Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Arch Resources announced its third-quarter 2023 results on October 25, 2023, for the period ending September 30, 2023. The company reported operating earnings per share (EPS) of $3.91, which surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.26 by 19.9%. In its Metallurgical segment, Arch Resources sold 2.3 million tons of coal, a 21.1% increase from the 1.9 million tons sold in the prior-year quarter. The Thermal segment sold 16.8 million tons of coal during the same period. <2> The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) announced on February 16, 2023, that it had sent a letter to Warrior Met Coal with an unconditional offer for striking miners to return to work. This move aimed to end the longest strike in Alabama's history, which commenced on April 1, 2021. The effective date for the miners' return was set for March 2, 2023. The strike, involving around 1,100 miners, was initiated over disagreements on a new labor contract. UMWA President Cecil Roberts stated that the decision to return to work marked a new phase in their efforts to secure a fair contract, as the prolonged strike had not resulted in significant changes. Warrior Met Coal accepted the offer, and the miners were to return under their previous contract while negotiations for a new agreement continued. <3> U.S. coal prices dropped significantly from record highs, with Northern Appalachia coal experiencing a 45% decrease to $115 a ton in the week ending January 6, 2023. [1, 2] This decline was primarily attributed to warmer winter weather, which led to a reduced demand for heating fuels. [1, 2] Spot prices for coal from Central Appalachia and the Illinois Basin also saw substantial decreases of 33% and 31%, respectively. [2] The price drop was also influenced by the expiration of some high-price contracts at the end of 2022 and buyers placing orders for future quarters with the anticipation of lower prices. [2] <4> A U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) report indicated that U.S. coal exports fell significantly in 2019, countering the Trump administration's efforts to support the domestic coal industry. Total exports declined by 20% from the previous year. A 14% drop was observed in the first nine months of the year. A primary driver for this downturn was the trade war with China; retaliatory Chinese tariffs imposed in February and April led to a halt in U.S. coal imports by China. This disruption in trade with China accounted for a substantial portion of the overall export reduction. In addition to the trade dispute, the decline also reflected a broader global market trend of soft demand and ample supply for coal. The majority of U.S. coal exports in 2019 were directed to India, Japan, the Netherlands, Brazil, and South Korea.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) announced on May 7, 2024, that members of Local Unions 2133 and 8982 had ratified a new five-year collective bargaining agreement with Crimson Oak Grove Resources, LLC. The contract covers over 400 union members working at the Oak Grove mine and associated facilities in Jefferson County. Key provisions of the agreement include significant wage increases and improvements in paid time off, with no alterations to the workers' health care or other benefits. <2> On April 30, 2024, the U.S. Department of Labor's Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) announced the findings of its March 2024 impact inspections. The inspections, conducted at 14 mines across 11 states, resulted in 199 violations and one safeguard. This initiative is part of a broader program targeting mines with persistent health and safety violations, which was established following the Upper Big Branch Mine disaster in April 2010 that killed 29 miners. <3> Based on first-quarter data from the Wyoming State Geological Survey, coal production in Wyoming's Powder River Basin fell by nearly 21% in the first quarter of 2024 compared to the same period in 2023. The total amount of coal mined dropped from over 58 million tons in Q1 2023 to more than 46 million tons in Q1 2024. Concurrently, employment in the basin's mines decreased by 101 jobs, bringing the total number of workers to 4,103 at the end of the quarter. <4> Alliance Resource Partners, L.P. (ARLP) reported its financial and operating results for the first quarter of 2024, which ended on March 31, 2024. The announcement was made on April 29, 2024. [3, 7] The company's total revenues for the quarter were $651.7 million, a slight decrease from the $662.9 million reported in the first quarter of 2023. [2, 3] Net income reached $158.1 million, or $1.21 per unit, and EBITDA was $235.0 million. [1, 3] The reported earnings per share of $1.21 surpassed analyst estimates. [2, 4] Key operational details include a 5.8% year-over-year increase in the average coal sales price in the Illinois Basin, while Appalachian prices saw a significant decrease of 19.4%. [3] Despite the drop in Appalachian prices, overall coal sales volumes increased by 2.4% compared to the prior year's first quarter. [1] Additionally, the company announced a quarterly cash distribution of $0.70 per unit. [1] <5> A report from the Wyoming State Geological Survey indicated a significant downturn in coal production in the state's Powder River Basin for the first quarter of 2024. [2] Production fell by nearly 21% compared to the first quarter of 2023, dropping from over 58 million tons to approximately 46 million tons. [2] This decline is part of a long-term trend attributed to several structural challenges, including the ongoing retirement of coal-fired power plants across the United States. [2] Competition from more affordable energy sources, particularly natural gas which has been at historically low prices, has also weakened demand for coal. [2] This situation is further compounded by new federal environmental regulations announced in April 2024, which are expected to accelerate the closure of coal plants. [2] The decreased demand has led to major coal operators in the region reporting lower volumes, with potential layoffs mentioned as a possibility. [2] <6> On April 18, 2024, the U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) published a final rule to enhance protections for miners against respirable crystalline silica. This rule lowers the permissible exposure limit (PEL) for all miners from 100 to 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, calculated as an 8-hour time-weighted average. It also establishes a new action level of 25 micrograms, which triggers a requirement for corrective measures. Key provisions of the rule mandate that mine operators use engineering controls to limit dust exposure, conduct environmental monitoring, and for metal and nonmetal mines, establish medical surveillance programs similar to those already in place for coal mines. <7> In its April 2024 Short-Term Energy Outlook, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) revised its forecast for U.S. coal exports in direct response to the closure of the Port of Baltimore following the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge on March 26, 2024. The agency projected that coal exports would decrease by 33% in April and 20% in May compared to its previous forecast. This adjustment marked a significant reversal from the EIA's earlier projection of a 1% increase in coal exports for 2024, with the new forecast anticipating a 6% decrease for the year. The Port of Baltimore is the second-largest hub for coal exports in the United States. <8> Following the conclusion of Alabama's longest strike, which ran from April 1, 2021, to February 16, 2023, the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) and the AFL-CIO presented a package of corporate governance reform proposals at the Warrior Met Coal annual shareholders' meeting. The unions urged stockholders to support five proposals, which notably included requiring stockholder approval for executive severance packages, or 'golden parachutes', and commissioning an independent, third-party assessment of the company's respect for workers' international human rights of freedom of association and collective bargaining. <9> In January 2024, the U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) performed impact inspections at 15 mines across 10 states, uncovering 188 violations. [1, 2] These inspections are specifically targeted at mines with histories of poor compliance, previous accidents, and other safety concerns. [1, 2] Out of the total violations found, 63 were designated as significant and substantial (S&S), and one received an unwarrantable failure finding. [1, 2] The U.S. Department of Labor announced the findings from these inspections on February 26, 2024. [1] <10> In late December 2023, analysts predicted a challenging year for the U.S. export and domestic thermal coal markets in 2024, citing expectations of mild global demand. [1] Export prices were anticipated to be backwardated, a market condition where the forward or futures price of a commodity is lower than the expected spot price. This outlook was influenced by several factors, including forecasts for warmer weather, an oversupply in the market, and significant competition from other coal-exporting nations. [2] Specifically, competitively priced coal from South Africa and declining petcoke prices were identified as key challenges for Northern Appalachian coal. [2] The sentiment for the domestic thermal coal market was mixed. While high stockpiles in the electric power sector put downward pressure on prices in 2023, there was potential for coal generation to become more competitive if natural gas prices were to rise in 2024. [2]

After weakening to a tropical storm over Georgia, Debby re-emerged into the Atlantic and made a second landfall as a subtropical storm in South Carolina on August 8. The storm's prolonged duration over the coast led to historic rainfall, with some areas in Florida receiving nearly 20 inches, resulting in significant flooding. The hurricane caused extensive power outages, affecting hundreds of thousands of customers across Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas. Significant disruptions to supply chains occurred, with the ports of Jacksonville, Savannah, and Brunswick experiencing closures to vessel traffic. President Joe Biden issued emergency declarations for Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas. Preliminary estimates place the total economic damage and loss in the United States in the billions of dollars. <2> NACCO Industries announced its financial results for the second quarter of 2024, reporting a consolidated net income of $6.0 million, or $0.81 per diluted share. [1] This represents a significant increase from the $2.5 million, or $0.34 per share, reported in the same period of 2023. [1] The operating profit saw a substantial rise to $7.4 million, compared to $1.8 million in the second quarter of the previous year, a figure that includes a $4.5 million gain from an asset sale. [1] A key driver of this improved performance was the significantly better operating results within the Coal Mining segment. This improvement occurred despite lower revenues, which were partly affected by reduced deliveries at the Mississippi Lignite Mining Company because a customer's power plant was operating at a reduced capacity. The company's overall financial health was also bolstered by strong results in the North American Mining segment and a gain on a land sale in the Minerals Management segment. [1] NACCO Industries hosted a conference call on August 1, 2024, to discuss these results. The agency forecast that prices would be approximately 36% higher in the second half of the year compared to the first half. This anticipated increase in natural gas costs was expected to make coal a more economical fuel source for utilities, leading to a projected 3% rise in coal-fired power generation during the same period to help meet a 2% growth in electricity demand. <5> In 2025, the U.S. is expected to see a significant increase in the retirement of coal-fired power plants. According to data from Argus Media, 34 coal-fired units are scheduled to shut down, which will remove approximately 14,532 megawatts of summer generating capacity. The retiring units are mostly located in the central and eastern U.S., within the MISO and PJM Interconnection territories. Notable closures include units at the J H Campbell plant in Michigan, Brandon Shores in Maryland, and the Intermountain Power Plant in Utah. Other sources, such as the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), also forecast a substantial increase in coal plant retirements for 2025, though their specific figures differ, projecting 8.1 GW of retired coal capacity. <6> The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) announced on May 7, 2024, that members of Local Unions 2133 and 8982 had ratified a new five-year collective bargaining agreement with Crimson Oak Grove Resources, LLC. The contract covers over 400 union members working at the Oak Grove mine and associated facilities in Jefferson County. Key provisions of the agreement include significant wage increases and improvements in paid time off, with no alterations to the workers' health care or other benefits. <7> On April 30, 2024, the U.S. Department of Labor's Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) announced the findings of its March 2024 impact inspections. The inspections, conducted at 14 mines across 11 states, resulted in 199 violations and one safeguard. This initiative is part of a broader program targeting mines with persistent health and safety violations, which was established following the Upper Big Branch Mine disaster in April 2010 that killed 29 miners. <8> Based on first-quarter data from the Wyoming State Geological Survey, coal production in Wyoming's Powder River Basin fell by nearly 21% in the first quarter of 2024 compared to the same period in 2023. The total amount of coal mined dropped from over 58 million tons in Q1 2023 to more than 46 million tons in Q1 2024. Concurrently, employment in the basin's mines decreased by 101 jobs, bringing the total number of workers to 4,103 at the end of the quarter. <9> Alliance Resource Partners, L.P. (ARLP) reported its financial and operating results for the first quarter of 2024, which ended on March 31, 2024. The announcement was made on April 29, 2024. [3, 7] The company's total revenues for the quarter were $651.7 million, a slight decrease from the $662.9 million reported in the first quarter of 2023. [2, 3] Net income reached $158.1 million, or $1.21 per unit, and EBITDA was $235.0 million. [1, 3] The reported earnings per share of $1.21 surpassed analyst estimates. [2, 4] Key operational details include a 5.8% year-over-year increase in the average coal sales price in the Illinois Basin, while Appalachian prices saw a significant decrease of 19.4%. [3] Despite the drop in Appalachian prices, overall coal sales volumes increased by 2.4% compared to the prior year's first quarter. [1] Additionally, the company announced a quarterly cash distribution of $0.70 per unit. [1] <10> A report from the Wyoming State Geological Survey indicated a significant downturn in coal production in the state's Powder River Basin for the first quarter of 2024. [2] Production fell by nearly 21% compared to the first quarter of 2023, dropping from over 58 million tons to approximately 46 million tons. [2] This decline is part of a long-term trend attributed to several structural challenges, including the ongoing retirement of coal-fired power plants across the United States. [2] Competition from more affordable energy sources, particularly natural gas which has been at historically low prices, has also weakened demand for coal. [2] This situation is further compounded by new federal environmental regulations announced in April 2024, which are expected to accelerate the closure of coal plants. [2] The decreased demand has led to major coal operators in the region reporting lower volumes, with potential layoffs mentioned as a possibility. [2]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In March 2025, U.S. coal prices experienced a 3.4% increase, a rebound attributed to strong demand from the nation's steel and power sectors. The demand from the steel industry was primarily driven by a rise in domestic crude steel production, which occurred amid the imposition of tariffs on steel imports. Further bolstering coal's demand, the U.S. Energy Information Administration had projected record-high power consumption for the first quarter of 2025, prompting increased use in electricity generation. <2> In February 2025, US coal prices experienced a slight decline of 0.8%; due to a significant increase in supply; with production reaching 10.6 million short tons in the last week of the month. <3> In the first quarter of 2025, the U.S. metallurgical coal market underwent a significant price correction, with the High Vol A Coking Coal FOB U.S. East Coast benchmark price falling to $172 per metric ton. [2] This sharp decline was attributed to a combination of weak global steel demand and uncertainties surrounding international trade policies. [2] <4> A report from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) announced that gross U.S. coal exports reached 10 million short tons in June 2024, marking the highest monthly total since October 2018. This figure was part of an upward trend in U.S. coal exports, which have increased annually since 2020. The exports consist of both steam coal, used for electricity generation, and metallurgical coal, used in steel production. The EIA's Short-Term Energy Outlook forecasts that U.S. coal exports will only surpass the 10 million short ton mark in December of 2025 and 2026. <5> Hallador Energy's subsidiary, Hallador Power Company, LLC, entered into a Conversion Transaction Commitment Agreement with a major global data center developer, which became effective on January 2, 2025. This agreement, announced on January 7, 2025, follows a non-binding term sheet from the third quarter of 2024. It grants the developer 105 business days of exclusive negotiations for a potential long-term contract to supply energy and capacity for a new data center in Indiana. If finalized, the deal is expected to contract the majority of Hallador's energy and capacity for over a decade at favorable rates. As part of the commitment, Hallador is set to receive up to $5 million in payments during the exclusivity period. <6> In a report released in December 2024, the International Energy Agency (IEA) projected that global demand for coal would reach a record 8.77 billion tons in 2024 before plateauing through 2027. The report highlighted divergent trends, with demand growing in China by 1% and India by over 5%. Conversely, usage in developed economies is expected to continue a structural decline, with demand in the United States and the European Union forecast to fall by 5% and 12% respectively in 2024. The IEA noted that much of the domestically consumed coal in the U.S. is secured through long-term contracts, which contributes to supply stability. <7> In a forecast published on October 24, 2024, ChemAnalyst predicted a marginal increase in U.S. coal prices for the month of October 2024. [2] The anticipated rise was attributed to several factors, primarily increased demand from coal-importing nations like India, where the onset of the Diwali festival season was expected to drive up energy needs. [2] The report also noted other conflicting market dynamics, including an announcement of U.S. government grants for green manufacturing in former coal communities, which could decrease long-term domestic demand. [2] Global supply factors, such as a forecasted cyclone season in Australia potentially impacting shipping, were also mentioned as possibly putting upward pressure on prices. [2] <8> On October 22, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced $428 million for 14 projects aimed at accelerating domestic clean energy manufacturing in 15 communities economically impacted by the closure of coal mines and power plants. This funding, part of the Biden-Harris Administration's Investing in America agenda and sourced from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, is the second round from the Advanced Energy Manufacturing and Recycling Program. The initiative is designed to bolster U.S. supply chains across five key areas: battery manufacturing and recycling, grid components, clean power generation, low-carbon materials, and energy efficiency products. The projects are expected to create over 1,900 jobs and leverage more than $500 million in private sector investment, signaling a continued policy of transitioning fossil fuel-based economies toward green manufacturing. <9> An analysis of U.S. metallurgical coal exports for August 2024 revealed a 17% year-on-year decline to 3.86 million tons. [3] This decrease was primarily attributed to reduced demand from key markets, including a 37% drop in shipments to India, which totaled 578,000 tons, and a 33% fall in exports to Brazil, amounting to 406,000 tons. The sharp decrease in metallurgical coal exports offset a rise in U.S. thermal coal exports during the same month. [3]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The U.S. Coal Show, a major biennial trade show and exhibition focusing on underground coal mining, is scheduled to take place in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, from June 3-5, 2025. Formerly known as Longwall USA, the event will be held at the David L. Lawrence Convention Center. It serves as a key platform for professionals in the coal industry, including executives, technical experts, and government officials, to explore the latest advancements in longwall and room and pillar mining equipment and technology. The show, organized by Mining Media International, will feature a wide range of exhibitors such as machine manufacturers, software providers, and safety equipment suppliers. In addition to the exhibition, the event offers educational and technical programs, providing a valuable opportunity for knowledge exchange and networking. <2> On April 8, 2025, the White House issued an executive order titled "Reinvigorating America's Beautiful Clean Coal Industry" to bolster the U.S. coal industry. [2, 5, 7] The order's stated policy is that coal is essential to the nation's economic and national security. [5] Key provisions include designating coal as a "mineral" under Executive Order 14241, which entitles it to benefits such as expedited permitting and potential federal financial support. [5, 7] The order directs federal agencies to remove regulatory barriers, prioritize coal leasing on federal lands, and rescind policies that favor a transition away from coal. [5, 6] It also aims to promote the export of U.S. coal and coal technologies and specifically mentions using coal to help power the increasing electrical demand from artificial intelligence data centers. [5, 6] <3> On April 2, 2025, a date the administration termed 'Liberation Day', the U.S. government announced a comprehensive package of new customs tariffs, invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). [1, 3] The plan included a baseline 10% tariff on nearly all imports, effective April 5, 2025, to be followed by higher, country-specific 'reciprocal' tariffs. [2, 5] The announcement created significant immediate uncertainty and a downturn in global markets, causing a sharp decline in U.S. equities and a fall in the U.S. dollar. [3, 10] This turmoil contributed to a decline in the energy complex, which intensified a market shift by industrial consumers, such as cement producers, away from petroleum coke and towards coal. [10] This trend was driven by a narrowing price discount for petcoke relative to coal that predated the announcement, with the tariff uncertainty and the availability of inexpensive Russian coal further weighing on petcoke demand. [6, 8] <4> In March 2025, U.S. coal prices experienced a 3.4% increase, a rebound attributed to strong demand from the nation's steel and power sectors. The demand from the steel industry was primarily driven by a rise in domestic crude steel production, which occurred amid the imposition of tariffs on steel imports. Further bolstering coal's demand, the U.S. Energy Information Administration had projected record-high power consumption for the first quarter of 2025, prompting increased use in electricity generation. <5> In February 2025, US coal prices experienced a slight decline of 0.8%; due to a significant increase in supply; with production reaching 10.6 million short tons in the last week of the month. <6> In the first quarter of 2025, the U.S. metallurgical coal market underwent a significant price correction, with the High Vol A Coking Coal FOB U.S. East Coast benchmark price falling to $172 per metric ton. [2] This sharp decline was attributed to a combination of weak global steel demand and uncertainties surrounding international trade policies. [2] <7> A report from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) announced that gross U.S. coal exports reached 10 million short tons in June 2024, marking the highest monthly total since October 2018. This figure was part of an upward trend in U.S. coal exports, which have increased annually since 2020. The exports consist of both steam coal, used for electricity generation, and metallurgical coal, used in steel production. The EIA's Short-Term Energy Outlook forecasts that U.S. coal exports will only surpass the 10 million short ton mark in December of 2025 and 2026. <8> Hallador Energy's subsidiary, Hallador Power Company, LLC, entered into a Conversion Transaction Commitment Agreement with a major global data center developer, which became effective on January 2, 2025. This agreement, announced on January 7, 2025, follows a non-binding term sheet from the third quarter of 2024. It grants the developer 105 business days of exclusive negotiations for a potential long-term contract to supply energy and capacity for a new data center in Indiana. If finalized, the deal is expected to contract the majority of Hallador's energy and capacity for over a decade at favorable rates. As part of the commitment, Hallador is set to receive up to $5 million in payments during the exclusivity period. <9> In a report released in December 2024, the International Energy Agency (IEA) projected that global demand for coal would reach a record 8.77 billion tons in 2024 before plateauing through 2027. The report highlighted divergent trends, with demand growing in China by 1% and India by over 5%. Conversely, usage in developed economies is expected to continue a structural decline, with demand in the United States and the European Union forecast to fall by 5% and 12% respectively in 2024. The IEA noted that much of the domestically consumed coal in the U.S. is secured through long-term contracts, which contributes to supply stability. <10> In a forecast published on October 24, 2024, ChemAnalyst predicted a marginal increase in U.S. coal prices for the month of October 2024. [2] The anticipated rise was attributed to several factors, primarily increased demand from coal-importing nations like India, where the onset of the Diwali festival season was expected to drive up energy needs. [2] The report also noted other conflicting market dynamics, including an announcement of U.S. government grants for green manufacturing in former coal communities, which could decrease long-term domestic demand. [2] Global supply factors, such as a forecasted cyclone season in Australia potentially impacting shipping, were also mentioned as possibly putting upward pressure on prices. [2]
